concept.body: Recipe: (1) open the compass past half of AB, (2) arc from A above and below, (3) same radius, arc from B — they cross at X and Y, (4) draw line XY. It works because X and Y are each the same distance from A and from B, and equidistant points sit on the perpendicular bisector.

explanationVariants: Because both arcs used the same radius, XA = XB — X is equidistant from the endpoints.
Equal compass radius from A and B is what forces XA = XB.

widget.prompt: In the perpendicular-bisector construction, why is XA = XB?

options.label: Both were drawn with the same compass radius
options.feedback: One unchanged opening swung from A and from B makes both distances equal.

options.label: Because X is the midpoint of AB
options.feedback: X sits OFF the segment, above it — the midpoint is where the finished line crosses AB.

options.label: Because AB was measured first
options.feedback: Nothing is measured — the equality comes from the equal radius, not a ruler.

options.label: Because X is closer to A
options.feedback: X is the SAME distance from each — that equality is the whole point.

steps.body: The workhorse construction. To bisect segment AB perpendicularly: open the compass **wider than half of AB**, swing an arc from A, swing the SAME radius from B, and connect the two crossing points. That line is the **perpendicular bisector** — it hits AB's midpoint at a right angle.

widget.prompt: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB. Reveal each stage.

panels.title: Arc from A
panels.body: Open past the midpoint. With the point on A, swing an arc reaching above and below AB.

panels.title: Same-radius arc from B
panels.body: Without changing the opening, swing from B. The two arcs cross at two points, X and Y.

panels.title: Draw line XY
panels.body: The straightedge line through X and Y is the perpendicular bisector — through the midpoint, at 90°.

widget.continueFeedback: Reveal each compass move in turn.
widget.successFeedback: Line XY bisects AB at a right angle.

widget.prompt: A and B are 6 apart. Open the compass until the two arcs actually meet — find the smallest whole radius that does it.
widget.successFeedback: Radius 4 — the first whole opening that clears half of 6. Widen it and watch: the crossings slide, but the LINE through them refuses to move. Both crossings are equidistant from A and from B by construction, so they lie on the perpendicular bisector no matter which radius you chose.
widget.lowFeedback: The arcs cannot reach each other yet. Each reaches only its own radius from its own end, so together they must span more than the 6 between A and B — the radius has to clear 3.
widget.highFeedback: They do meet, but you were asked for the SMALLEST whole radius that reaches. Come back down until they are just about to come apart.

predict.prompt: Both arcs will be drawn with the SAME compass opening — one from A, one from B. Whatever point they cross at must be…

options.label: The same distance from A and from B — that is what equal radii mean
Closer to whichever end the compass touched first

predict.reveal: An arc is every point at ONE distance from its center. Where two equal-radius arcs cross, that point is the same distance from A and from B at once — and every such point lies on the perpendicular bisector. The compass is not drawing a curve; it is making a promise about distance.

explanationVariants: If the radius were less than half of AB, the two arcs couldn't reach each other — they'd never cross, so there'd be no X or Y to draw the line through.
The arcs meet only when each reaches past the midpoint. Radius ≤ half means they fall short and miss.

widget.prompt: Why must the compass be opened WIDER than half of AB?

options.label: Otherwise the two arcs are too short to cross
options.feedback: Below half, the arcs can't reach the middle to meet — no crossing points, no bisector line.

options.label: Otherwise the bisector wouldn't be perpendicular
options.feedback: Any equal-radius pair gives a PERPENDICULAR result — the width only controls whether the arcs meet at all.

options.label: So the midpoint lands exactly at the center
options.feedback: The midpoint is determined by AB, not the compass width — width just needs to be big enough for arcs to cross.

options.label: To make the two arcs different sizes
options.feedback: The arcs must be the SAME size (same radius). Width only needs to exceed half so they reach each other.

widget.prompt: On a number line, A sits at coordinate 70 and B at 210. The perpendicular bisector crosses AB at its midpoint. What coordinate is that?

commonErrors.feedback: 280 is 70 + 210 — coordinates summed. The midpoint is their AVERAGE: (70 + 210)/2 = 140.
70 is endpoint A. The bisector meets AB halfway between the endpoints: 140.

steps.body: **Why it works** is the real lesson. Both X and Y were drawn at the same radius from A AND from B, so XA = XB and YA = YB. A point equidistant from A and B must lie on the perpendicular bisector — so the line through X and Y IS it.

explanationVariants: X was swung at one radius from both A and B, so XA = XB — X is equidistant, hence on the perpendicular bisector. Same for Y.
Equal radii force XA = XB; the set of points equidistant from A and B is exactly the perpendicular bisector.

widget.prompt: What property of X and Y proves line XY is the perpendicular bisector of AB?

options.label: Each of X and Y is equidistant from A and B
options.feedback: Same radius from A and from B gives XA = XB and YA = YB — and equidistant points lie on the perpendicular bisector.

options.label: X and Y are the midpoints of the two arcs
options.feedback: Arc midpoints aren't what's used — it's that X and Y sit at EQUAL distances from A and B.

options.label: X and Y are each twice as far from A as from B
options.feedback: The radii are EQUAL, not doubled — XA = XB exactly, which is what puts them on the bisector.

options.label: XY is parallel to AB
options.feedback: XY is PERPENDICULAR to AB, not parallel — it crosses AB at the midpoint at 90°.

hints: The construction produces a line with two features at once.
It passes through the midpoint AND meets AB at 90°.
So it can be used any time you need EITHER the midpoint OR a right angle on AB.
explanationVariants: The perpendicular bisector both finds the midpoint of AB and erects a right angle to AB — so the same construction bisects a segment AND drops/raises a perpendicular.
Two jobs, one recipe: midpoint (bisector) and 90° (perpendicular). That's why it's the workhorse.

widget.prompt: You need to construct the MIDPOINT of a segment — no perpendicular required. Which construction gives it to you?

options.label: A perpendicular bisector meets the segment at its midpoint.
options.feedback: Even when you only want the midpoint, the perpendicular bisector delivers it where it meets the segment.

options.label: Copying the segment onto a new ray gives its midpoint.
options.feedback: Copying reproduces the length elsewhere but never marks the middle of the original.

options.label: One arc from an endpoint marks the segment’s midpoint.
options.feedback: One arc gives points at a fixed distance from ONE endpoint — not the balanced middle. You need arcs from both.

options.label: A straightedge through the endpoints marks the midpoint.
options.feedback: That just redraws the segment itself — it marks no interior point.

takeaways: Equal arcs from both endpoints cross at two points; their line is the perpendicular bisector.
Open wider than half so the arcs can meet.
It works because those crossing points are equidistant from A and B — and it gives midpoint AND right angle.
steps.teaser: Next: swing arcs INSIDE an angle to split it exactly in half.
